title: Orcas Are Smashing Sunfish Like Piñatas!
summary:
Imagine a giant fish the size of a small car. Now imagine a killer whale ramming into it so hard the fish EXPLODES. That's exactly what scientists filmed in the Gulf of California in 2024 and 2025.

Here's how it worked: one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca slammed into it with enough force to smash it to smithereens. Smithereens means tiny little pieces!

Why would orcas do this? Scientists have two big ideas. First, breaking a huge sunfish into small bites could help feed young orcas. After one explosion, a baby orca ate the little bits. Second, orcas might just find it fun. They're super smart and playful animals.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist in New Zealand who watched the videos. That means she was totally shocked and amazed. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen."

Orcas are famous for clever hunting tricks. They work as a team to ambush blue whales and whale sharks. They even make waves to knock penguins off ice floes!

Sharp-tail sunfish can grow up to 10 feet long — longer than a grown-up is tall. That's a big meal to break apart.

The scientists shared their findings on July 23 in a journal called Frontiers in Ethology. Ethology is the science of animal behavior.

So next time you see an orca, remember: it might be a hunter, a parent, or just a whale looking for a little fun.
why_it_matters: It shows that animals can be clever and playful in ways we never guessed, and that watching nature closely — even with a camera — can teach us brand-new things.

background_read: The Gulf of California (the long, narrow sea between Mexico's mainland and the Baja California peninsula) is famous for its rich sea life, including many kinds of whales, dolphins and fish.
Orcas swim in every ocean on Earth, and they are actually the largest members of the dolphin family — not whales at all.

Marianne Nyegaard (a scientist in New Zealand who studies ocean sunfish) watched the videos and helped make sure the scientists understood what they were seeing. Scientists publish studies like this in journals such as Frontiers in Ethology, where other experts check the work first.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists, including marine biologist Marianne Nyegaard in New Zealand, who studied videos of orcas in the Gulf of California.
WHAT: Two adult orcas worked together — one held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady while the other slammed into it and smashed it into tiny pieces.
WHERE: The Gulf of California, the sea between Mexico's mainland and the Baja California peninsula, in 2024 and 2025.
WHY: Scientists think the orcas may be breaking up a giant fish so their babies can eat small bites — or they may simply find it fun, since orcas are smart and playful.

perspectives.description: Researchers said they were 'gobsmacked' and called it the coolest thing they had ever seen, because no one had filmed orcas smashing a sunfish this way before.
Scientists have two ideas — feeding the babies or just having fun — and they admit they cannot prove which one is right yet, so they need more videos.
The same event looks very different depending on who you are: an exciting hunt for the orcas, but a very bad day for the huge sunfish that got smashed apart.
